The Common vole (Microtus arvalis) is a small arvicoline rodent widely distributed across European grasslands and agricultural landscapes, where its life history traits reflect a classic r-selected strategy tuned to high population turnover. At birth, the altricial neonate typically weighs around 1.43 grams [Wwb = around 1.43 grams], a remarkably small mass that underscores the substantial energetic investment required during the ensuing lactation period. Although this value is consistently reported, some studies, such as those conducted by Sawi in 1970, have documented a slightly higher neonatal mass closer to 1.88 grams [Wwb = 1.88 grams], suggesting that intraspecific variation in maternal condition or litter size may influence birth weight across different populations. This initial mass is just a fraction of the ultimate adult size that the animal will eventually achieve, setting the stage for a period of rapid growth. The species' high reproductive potential is a well-known feature of its ecology, contributing to its capacity for dramatic population fluctuations. The developmental trajectory from this diminutive newborn to a fully grown adult proceeds through several well-defined stages, each marked by distinct morphological and physiological thresholds.

Under controlled thermal conditions maintained at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the duration of gestation in the Common vole lasts for 21 days [tg = 21 days], a relatively brief period that is characteristic of many small-bodied microtine rodents. This short gestation is followed by a rapid postnatal development sequence that is tightly coupled to the same ambient temperature regime. After parturition, the pre-weaning pup undergoes a period of exclusive lactation that culminates in nutritional independence, with weaning occurring at 13.7 days after birth [tx = 13.7 days after birth] at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. Strikingly, the transition to puberty is not delayed beyond this point; the weaned young become reproductively mature almost immediately, with the time since birth at puberty also recorded at 13.7 days since birth [tp = 13.7 days since birth] under these same laboratory conditions at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This compressed developmental schedule — where weaning and sexual maturation are effectively simultaneous — represents an extreme life history adaptation that allows population densities to increase explosively when environmental conditions are favorable. The rapid attainment of reproductive competence at such a young age, literally as soon as the young begin to feed independently, is a key factor underlying the Common vole's notorious population cycles.

The body mass trajectory of the Common vole is characterized by a steep growth curve that quickly elevates the animal from its neonatal weight to the threshold required for reproductive competence. The wet weight at puberty for this species is approximately 9 grams [Wwp = approximately 9 grams], a mass that is attained almost immediately after weaning given the compressed developmental schedule. Interestingly, this value is essentially identical to the wet weight at weaning, which is also recorded as approximately 9 grams [Wwx = approximately 9 grams], reinforcing the observation that the nutritional transition to solid food and the onset of gonadal maturation occur concurrently. Beyond this stage, continued somatic growth leads to an ultimate adult body size, with the maximum wet weight achieved by reproductively active adults reaching around 50 grams [Wwi = around 50 grams]. This final adult mass from the 1.43 gram [Wwb = 1.43 gram] neonate demonstrates a remarkable growth capacity that is fueled by the high-quality forage available in managed grasslands. The attainment of such a comparatively large adult body size from a very small birth weight within a span of just a few weeks is a defining feature of the species' energy-intensive life history.

Reproductive output in the Common vole is correspondingly high, reflecting its status as one of the most fecund small mammals in temperate Eurasia. Field surveys conducted in Germany during 1980 examined solitary females and documented that, when maintained at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], females produce an average of approximately 4 to 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 4 to 5 pups per litter] and successfully raise approximately 3 to 4 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 to 4 litters per year]. This figure captures the total annual reproductive output under optimal thermal conditions, integrating both litter size and the frequency of successive parturitions over the course of a breeding season. It is worth noting that this rate can be decomposed into distinct components: each pregnancy yields an average litter, and the short generation time allows for multiple breeding events each year. The high value reflects both the large number of pups produced per reproductive event and the rapid succession of litters that the female can sustain. This extraordinary fecundity, combined with the early age at first reproduction, explains how Common vole populations can transition from low densities to plague levels within a single growing season, causing significant damage to agricultural crops and pastures across their range.

The life history strategy of the Common vole, with its extreme precocial reproductive maturation and high annual fecundity, positions it as a highly adaptable colonizer of ephemeral habitats. In comparative terms, the species' suite of life history parameters — a neonatal mass of about 1.43 grams [Wwb = about 1.43 grams], a weaning mass of roughly 9 grams [Wwx = roughly 9 grams], and an ultimate adult mass of 50 grams [Wwi = 50 grams] — highlights the efficiency of its rapid growth trajectory. The very short intervals from birth to weaning and puberty, both clocking in at 13.7 days from birth [tp = 13.7 days from birth] [tx = at 13.7 days from birth] under the standard 37 °C [T = 37 °C] regime, are among the shortest recorded for any eutherian mammal of comparable adult size, with the brief 21-day gestation (21 days) [tg = 21 days] further compressing the generation cycle. This compressed schedule places Microtus arvalis among the fastest-maturing eutherians, with growth and reproductive development completing within the span of a single synodic month. From a population ecology perspective, the ability to produce approximately 4 to 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 4 to 5 pups per litter] across multiple litters per year [F_R_i = multiple litters per year] under favorable thermal conditions creates the potential for exponential population growth. Understanding these core life history parameters is essential for modeling population outbreaks and for developing effective management strategies for this keystone prey species and agricultural pest.
